facts.fact: Acrylic is softer than glass and scratches more easily.
A scratch on the outside of the tank is easier to fix than one on the inside; inside repairs may mean taking out the fish and water.
Some scratches are faint, so check the panels regularly under good light.
Fingernail test: if your nail catches on a scratch, it is probably too deep to polish out easily.
White crust along the waterline is limescale: minerals left on the glass when water evaporates.
Common causes of tank scratches are gravel scraping the panel, metal scrubbers and accidental knocks.
Sand or grit trapped in a magnetic cleaner's pad can leave a permanent scratch.
Some dark sands contain magnetic particles, so take extra care with a magnet cleaner near the substrate.
A dull razor blade is what scratches glass, so change the blade when it starts to drag.
Topping off with untreated water adds more minerals each time, which builds up hard-water stains.
Clean the inside glass before the water change, so loosened algae leaves with the old water.
Before each use, check the magnet cleaner's pad for sand or grit.
Choose a magnetic cleaner rated for your glass thickness; a magnet made for thinner glass grips thick glass poorly and slips.
Move the magnet cleaner slowly in straight lines so no algae is missed.
Use a hand scraper for corners, the substrate line and other spots the magnet cannot reach.
For routine algae use a plastic blade; use a metal blade only on glass and only for tough deposits.
For green spot algae on glass, keep the razor blade flat against the glass at a low angle so it does not gouge.
Outside glass: a damp microfibre cloth usually removes fingerprints and dust; finish with a dry cloth.
If you use glass cleaner outside, spray it onto the cloth, not the glass, so overspray cannot drip in through gaps in the lid.
Hard-water stains: press a cloth soaked in undiluted white vinegar on the stain for 10–15 minutes, then wipe or scrape; repeat for stubborn stains.
For old, heavy lime deposits, soften them with vinegar first, then scrape at a shallow angle with a razor blade (glass tanks only).
Light scratch on glass: clean the spot with a soft damp cloth, rub polishing compound in gently in circles, rinse, and repeat if needed.
Light scratch on acrylic: clean the spot, apply acrylic scratch remover in circles, then buff with a second clean soft cloth.
Cerium oxide for glass scratches: mix it with water into a thin slurry and buff with a pad; mist with water or more slurry so the glass does not get hot.
Micro-Mesh acrylic kit: work through grits 1800, 2400, 3200, 4000, 6000 and 8000 in order, ending at 8000.
Micro-Mesh starting grit: 4000 or 6000 for very fine scratches, 2400 or 3200 for hairlines and light scuffs, and 320 wet/dry sandpaper for scratches a fingernail can feel.
Sand acrylic in straight lines, not circles; turn the sanding direction 90° with each new grit; and spread the sanding over 4 to 6 inches instead of sanding one spot.
Work on 1 to 1.5 square feet of acrylic at a time, overlapping slightly; sanding wet gives the best finish.
Novus on acrylic: start with the lightest product that works (#1, then #2, then #3 for deeper scratches); polish with strokes at right angles to the scratch, then finish with #1.
Test Novus #2 and #3 on a hidden spot first.
Deep scratches in glass: sand with very fine waterproof sandpaper plus polishing compound, starting with the finest grit and going rougher only if needed.
Get professional help for cracks or deep scratches that will not polish out.
Cerium oxide is for glass only; for acrylic tanks, sand and then use plastic polish.
Micro-Mesh says its abrasives can be used inside the tank with water and fish in place, but acrylic dust may contaminate the water, so it advises removing the water and fish first.
A BRS staff answer says Novus should be used only on the outside of a filled acrylic tank, and inside only when the tank is empty and dry.
Another BRS staff answer says Novus is safe inside a tank if it is rinsed and wiped off thoroughly before setup.
Micro-Mesh anti-static cream is for the outside only; wipe it off quickly and do not let it dry on the surface.
If you clean limescale with vinegar, take the fish out first and put them in a prepared temporary tank.
Vinegar changes the water's pH, which can stress fish, damage their slime coat or kill them; rinse away every trace before refilling.
Use only diluted white vinegar to clean a tank; other vinegars can contain impurities such as yeast or sulfites.
Chemical limescale removers made for the bathroom or sink are toxic to fish and must never be used in an aquarium.
Using household glass cleaner inside the tank: the ammonia and surfactants in it are toxic to fish and invertebrates.
Cleaning with a kitchen sponge that has touched soap or detergent, which can leave a deadly residue.
Never use razor blades, metal scrapers or green Scotch-Brite pads on acrylic; they scratch it.
The Tetra GS 45 scraper has a stainless steel blade and is not suitable for plastic or acrylic tanks.
The ADA Pro Razor is for glass tanks only, never acrylic.
Letting vinegar drip into a filled tank; it lowers pH.
Leaving stains too long makes them harder to remove.
Using metal scrubbers or other abrasive tools on the panels.
Use non-abrasive pads or sponges made for aquariums, handle decorations gently, and clean often so you never need heavy scrubbing.
On acrylic, use plastic scrapers, a credit card or acrylic-safe pads, and check magnet cleaners for grit even more carefully.
For acrylic tanks, use a magnet cleaner labelled safe for acrylic.
A plastic mesh cover on the magnet traps sand in its grooves so it does not touch the panel; replace it when worn.
Top off evaporated water regularly and check GH and KH to limit limescale.
Suggested schedule: inside glass once or twice a week, outside glass about weekly, hard-water stains monthly.
When chloramine in tap water breaks down, naturally or with a dechlorinator, it releases ammonia; leaving water to stand does not remove chloramine.
WikiHow says that for a scratch on the inside of a tank it is better to leave it alone and turn the tank so it shows less, instead of polishing it.
Vietnamese shop blogs call the algae tool 'dụng cụ vệ sinh tảo' (razor-shaped) and also mention 'bột tẩy rửa kính bể cá đa năng' (multi-purpose aquarium glass cleaning powder).
Vietnamese shops sell gravel vacuums for water changes under the name 'Ống Hút Cặn Thay Nước Cho Bể Cá'.
